title: What a Database Is
objective: After this level you can explain how a database stores records in tables and uses an index to find one among billions.
summary: A database keeps records as rows in tables, with typed columns that give the data meaning, and an index that jumps straight to one row instead of scanning them all.

cards.headline: A computer just found your order in a blink. It didn't read every one.
cards.body: Shops, banks and apps keep their records in databases: collections of data organized so a computer can search them and pull out one entry fast. Chapter 7 is about your data, so start with where it lives. How do you find one row among a mountain of them?

cards.headline: Tables: rows and columns
cards.body: The most popular kind, the relational database, stores data in tables, much like a spreadsheet. Each row is one record, say one customer, and each column is one field of that record: name, address, date joined. The columns are fixed; the rows come and go. Sign up for a new app and, somewhere, a table grows by exactly one row. That row is you.

cards.headline: Every column has a type
cards.body: Each column also has a data type, such as whole numbers, text or dates. The type limits what can go in the column and gives the stored data its meaning, so the database knows a number column can be added up and a date column can be compared with other dates. The same bits in a text column would just be letters. The table's design tells the database how to read every cell.

cards.fact: Without an index, a database must check every row, one by one.
cards.context: An index works like the one at the back of a book: look up the term, flip straight to the page. A database index keeps one column's values in sorted order, each pointing to its row, so searching it is much faster than searching the table. The price is upkeep: every change to the table must update the index too, so indexes nobody uses get removed.

cards.headline: Databases: found
learned: A database organizes data for fast search and retrieval
Tables hold records as rows and fields as columns
Each column's data type gives its data meaning
An index jumps straight to a row instead of scanning every one

questions.prompt: In a relational database table, what does each row hold?

options.label: A single column's worth of values
options.rationale: A column runs down the table; a row runs across it.

options.label: One record, such as one customer
An index of the whole table
options.rationale: An index is kept separately from the rows.

questions.explanation: Each row is one record and each column is a field of that record.

questions.prompt: How does a database index let the system find one record without checking every row?

options.label: It keeps the whole table in the processor's cache
options.rationale: An index is a separate lookup structure, not a copy in cache.

options.label: It deletes rows that nobody has searched for lately
It looks the value up in a sorted list that points straight to the row
It guesses the row's position from the size of the table
options.rationale: It looks the value up; it doesn't guess.

questions.explanation: An index keeps a column's values sorted, each pointing to its row, like a book's index points to pages.

questions.prompt: Level 10 said the same bits can mean different things. In a database table, what tells the system how to read the bits in a cell?

options.label: The order the rows were added
options.rationale: Row order doesn't change what a value means.

options.label: The speed of the storage drive
options.rationale: Speed affects how fast data arrives, not what it means.

options.label: The size of the index
options.rationale: An index helps find rows; it doesn't give them meaning.

questions.explanation: Each column's data type assigns meaning to the data stored in it, just as context decides what bytes mean.
